title: GitHub - chrchr/clanking: Turn agent activity into a quiet soundscape.
excerpt: Turn agent activity into a quiet soundscape. Contribute to chrchr/clanking development by creating an account on GitHub.
content_html:
What's that Clanking sound?

For machines called "clankers", LLM agents sure don't make much noise. Are they too quiet? Yes! But not anymore.

Clanking turns your LLM agents' activity into a subtle soundscape. It signals when an agent is working, waiting for input, or in another state. Clanking plays cues from many agents at once and harmonizes them into a happy chorus of chattering clankers.

Demo

demo.mp4

Design

Coding agent hooks invoke the Clanking CLI, which reads each hook event and plays a sound cue. For tool calls, it plays a short tick on one of several notes to signal that the agent is active. Other sounds indicate that the agent is outputting a response, waiting for input or permission, has finished, or has encountered an error.

Clanking runs as a daemon that starts on its first invocation, and the CLI sends messages to the background task on subsequent invocations. Sounds are quantized to sixteenth notes at the configured tempo, which defaults to 120 BPM. During high activity, Clanking switches to thirty-second notes. The program synthesizes the sounds.

Clanking uses stereo position to help you distinguish agent sessions. It positions each session according to the agent's working directory, so clanks from different sessions seem to come from different places.

You can configure the tempo and root note from the command line or Clanking's GTK 4 UI.

Installation

Clanking requires a Unix-like system with PipeWire and the pw-cat utility. It has an optional GTK 4 user interface for configuration. Clanking is vibe-coded in Go and requires a Go toolchain and GTK 4 development libraries to build.

On a Unix-like system with the required dependencies and an XDG-style desktop (such as GNOME or KDE), make install installs clanking, clanking-ui, a desktop file, and an icon in your home directory.

The included Containerfile lets you build Clanking without installing all the development dependencies on your system. The podman-make script builds and runs the container. Adapting it for Docker is left as an exercise for the reader or the reader's coding agent.

Configure your Coding Agents

With clanking and pw-cat in your $PATH on a system with PipeWire, you can configure your coding agent to invoke Clanking.

For Claude, install the Clanking plugin from this repository's marketplace:

/plugin install clanking --marketplace chrchr/clanking

For Codex, add this repository as a plugin marketplace:

codex plugin marketplace add chrchr/clanking
codex plugin add clanking@clanking

Restart Codex, then run /hooks. Trust the Clanking hooks.

Inspo

  • Peep (The Network Auralizer): Monitoring Your Network With Sound by Michael Gilfix and Prof. Alva Couch, Tufts University.

  • Star Trek: The Next Generation. The voice-interactive computer in the "Star Trek" franchise uses nonverbal sounds to signal that it is doing something.

  • Earcons (Wikipedia). "An earcon is a brief, distinctive sound that represents a specific event or conveys other information."
